description: Dillahunty argues that forgiving a mass murderer while eternally punishing victims disconnects ultimate outcomes from proportional desert, undermining Knechtle’s reconciliation of divine love and wrath.
critique: Strongest feature: The murderer-victim reversal directly engages Knechtle’s contention that wrath prevents indifference toward wrongdoing, because forgiving the perpetrator while eternally punishing victims makes ultimate outcomes appear disconnected from proportional desert. Principal limitation: Dillahunty presents a doctrinal hypothetical without establishing that Knechtle’s theology assigns either destiny as alleged, while calling Christian justice a bizarre lie, grossly immoral, and embarrassing greatly exceeds the argument’s compressed support. Live burden: He must specify how repentance, belief, culpability, forgiveness, and further judgment determine both destinies, then show that doctrinal qualifications cannot restore proportionate justice. Locked score: The score of 76 fits an exceptionally responsive, burden-relevant challenge with a lucid contrast, while discounting unverified assumptions, incomplete specification, and uncharitable certainty.
